statement: How many four-member teams can be chosen from ten people?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the ten people by the four places, which counts neither orderings nor selections.
I divided the ordered count by 7 rather than by the 24 orderings of four people.
I counted the ordered selections and never divided out the orderings within a team.
I allowed each of the four places to be filled by any of the ten, repeating people.

hints: A team has no internal order.
Count the ordered picks first, then divide by the number of ways the chosen four could be arranged, since each team was counted once for every arrangement.
10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040 ordered picks, and each team of four appears 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 times.

solutions.reliable: Ordered picks give 10 x 9 x 8 x 7 = 5040, and each team appears in all 24 of its orderings, so the count is 5040 / 24 = 210. The transferable idea: overcount in a way you can measure exactly, then divide by that measured overcount.
solutions.elegant: Choosing four to include is the same as choosing six to leave out, so the two calculations must agree.

whyOnTest: Selections are arrangements divided by the internal orderings, and the undivided count is the distractor that catches a rushed answer.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
